questions.q: What is a surface-code decoder's job, precisely?
options: To re-encode the logical qubit from scratch after every round
To physically prevent errors from ever occurring on the data qubits
To infer the most likely physical error chain from the full history of measured syndromes, then compute the correction needed to undo it
To measure the logical qubit's amplitudes directly
questions.explain: A decoder's job is inference from syndrome data to a likely error hypothesis, followed by computing the corresponding correction -- a strictly harder task than the chapter 3 lookup tables because of the surface code's scale and multi-round data.

questions.q: What is minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) used for in surface-code decoding?
options: Deciding how many ancilla qubits to place on the lattice
Measuring every data qubit directly to check its exact state
Choosing which classical code to use for the CSS construction
Pairing up defects (persistent syndrome flips) with each other or the lattice boundary at the lowest total cost, to infer the most likely error chain
questions.explain: MWPM treats defects as graph nodes and finds the lowest-cost pairing among them (or to the boundary), which corresponds to the most likely underlying error chain.

questions.q: Why does the lesson connect MWPM to the CSS construction from chapter 4 as both being 'reused classical machinery'?
options: Both let quantum error correction reuse existing, well-studied classical algorithms/theory instead of inventing entirely new machinery from scratch
Classical algorithms are never used anywhere in quantum error correction
MWPM was invented specifically and only for the surface code
MWPM and CSS codes are mathematically identical constructions
questions.explain: Just as CSS codes reuse classical coding theory for X and Z errors, MWPM reuses an existing classical graph algorithm for decoding -- a recurring theme of practical quantum error correction leaning on established classical tools.

questions.q: Why does decoding speed, not just accuracy, matter for a practical surface-code implementation?
options: Decoding only happens once at the very end of a computation, so speed never matters
Syndrome extraction runs continuously; if decoding can't keep pace with incoming syndrome data, a backlog builds and error correction falls behind the hardware it's meant to protect
Slow decoders only affect the Steane code, never the surface code
Decoding speed is irrelevant as long as the final answer is eventually correct
questions.explain: Because syndrome rounds keep arriving continuously during a live computation, a decoder that can't process them fast enough creates a growing backlog -- an honest, current open engineering challenge, not a solved problem.

questions.q: According to the lesson, is real-time surface-code decoding at the scale needed for useful fault-tolerant computation a solved, off-the-shelf capability today?
options: No -- keeping decoding latency low enough at genuinely useful lattice sizes is an active area of engineering research
Decoding speed was never actually a concern raised in the lesson
Yes, but only for lattices smaller than distance 3
Yes -- this has been fully solved and is a standard, routine capability on current hardware
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames real-time, large-scale decoding as an open, active research challenge, consistent with this course's honesty requirement about the current state of fault-tolerant computing.
